parts.text:
**"The Mom Test"** is a highly celebrated business concept and the title of a popular book by Rob Fitzpatrick (*"The Mom Test: How to talk to customers & learn if your business is a good idea when everyone is lying to you"*). 

It is a framework for conducting customer discovery and market research. The core premise is that **most people will lie to you (or at least sugarcoat the truth) to protect your feelings—especially your mom.** 

If you ask someone, *"I have an idea for an app that does X, do you think it's a good idea?"*, they will almost always say *"Yes, that sounds great!"* out of politeness. This leads to **false validation**, causing entrepreneurs to waste months or years building products that nobody actually wants or is willing to pay for.

The "Mom Test" provides a set of rules to design questions so that **even your mom couldn't lie to you.**

---

### The 3 Golden Rules of The Mom Test

To get honest, actionable data from potential customers, you must follow three simple rules:

#### 1. Talk about their life, instead of your idea
Do not pitch your product, and don't even mention your business idea. If you tell someone your idea, they will shift into "evaluation mode" and try to be encouraging. Instead, ask them about their current workflows, daily lives, and the problems they actually experience.

#### 2. Ask about specifics in the past, instead of generics or opinions about the future
People are terrible at predicting their future behavior, but they cannot lie about their past actions. 
* **Never ask:** *"Would you buy a product that did X?"* or *"How often would you use this?"*
* **Instead, ask:** *"How do you currently solve this problem?"* or *"Can you walk me through the last time you tried to do X?"*

#### 3. Talk less and listen more
Your goal is not to convince them that they have a problem or that your solution is great. Your goal is to listen and discover if they *already* care about the problem you are trying to solve.

---

### Examples: Bad Questions vs. Good Questions

| Bad Question (Invites Lies/Opinions) | Good Question (Uncovers Facts) | Why the Good Question is Better |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| "Do you think a calendar app for fitness would be a good idea?" | "How do you currently keep track of your workouts?" | Focuses on actual current behavior, not theoretical interest. |
| "Would you pay $10/month for this?" | "What are you currently spending to solve this problem?" | Reveals if they actually allocate a budget to this issue, rather than guessing what they might pay. |
| "How often do you go to the gym?" | "How many times did you go to the gym last week?" | Avoids generic self-idealization ("I go three times a week!") and gets hard, historical facts. |
| "Would you use a feature that does X?" | "How do you handle X right now? What have you tried in the past?" | Shows if the problem is painful enough that they’ve actively searched for a workaround. |

---

### Other Crucial Takeaways from the Framework

* **Compliments are worthless:** If a customer says, *"I love it!"* or *"You're so smart!"*, you have failed the interview. Compliments are the ultimate false positive. When you receive a compliment, you must politely deflect it and steer the conversation back to concrete facts.
* **Look for Commitment:** True validation doesn't come from nice words; it comes from **commitment**. At the end of a conversation, ask for a clear next step that requires a sacrifice from them, such as:
  * **Time commitment:** *"Can we schedule a 20-minute follow-up next Tuesday to look at a prototype?"*
  * **Reputational commitment:** *"Would you be willing to introduce me to your head of purchasing?"*
  * **Financial commitment:** A pre-order, deposit, or letter of intent. 
  If they make excuses to avoid these commitments, they aren't actually interested.
* **Keep it Casual:** You don't need a formal, 30-minute slide presentation to do customer discovery. Some of the best "Mom Test" interviews happen casually over coffee, lasting only 5 to 10 minutes, because the other person doesn't even realize they are being interviewed.
